source.title: Information FOMO: The unhealthy fear of missing out on information. A method for removing misleading data for healthier models

record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps the number of training samples and measures test errors under standard training, directly testing sample-wise double descent in new surrogate-model settings. It also compares this with data selection that aims to suppress the effect.
record.gate_note: The paper describes model-size and epoch-wise double descent in its introduction and figure 1, but does not report its own sweeps over those axes. The results cited from other work are not included as rows. The paper’s own results on standard training and FOMO-selected data are recorded below.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps training-sample count under standard random sampling for GP regression on a 1D function and a DeepONet on an 8D wave model, and reports test error. Rising error with more samples bears directly on V3 in new, non-classification regression settings. The FOMO comparisons test the authors' own selection method, not the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also argue that sample-wise double descent here reflects map complexity and sample distribution, not an under-to-over-parameterization crossover. They present FOMO as eliminating it, cutting median normalized MSE from about 20% to 1%.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses sample-count sweeps and test-error measurements in GP regression and an MMT DeepONet task, alongside a new sequential data-selection method. It does not reproduce the original study’s full set of model-size, epoch, and sample-size experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: For GP, the reported severity varies with nonlinear coefficient L: L = 0 has fast convergence without double descent, while nonzero coefficients show double descent, more severely for larger L. FOMO-selected data avoids the reported instability. For the DNN, the ensemble size changes how many samples are selected: N = 2 chooses approximately 25% more samples than N = 10, while median and range of both error metrics are described as nearly identical.

fits_no_version.finding: Sample-wise double descent in GP regression appears at 5–30 samples although the GP has only 2–3 hyperparameters. Its severity scales with the nonlinearity and extremes of the target map, and it is absent for a linear map.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample-wise double descent can be driven by target-map complexity and the input-sample distribution rather than by an under-to-over-parameterization crossover.

record.code_released: The text says GP code is provided via a Google Colaboratory link and DNN code via a Dropbox link; the URLs are not stated in the supplied text.
record.problems: The plotted error curves provide the main evidence, and exact curve values are not stated in the text. The experiments concern particular synthetic and physical regression tasks; the paper itself notes that performance in sufficiently noisy data and pathological cases remains for future work.

untested.parts: No effective-complexity predictor is tested. The authors only argue that the GP peak (5–30 samples) does not match parameter-count crossover.
Label-noise and regularization dependence are untested. The authors state, without showing, that a nonzero GP noise term would remove the instability.

missing.what: Location of the GP sample-wise peak (about 5–30 samples) relative to the GP's 2–3 tunable parameters, the authors' evidence that the peak is not at the interpolation threshold

record.verdict_notes: FOMO rows are the authors' own mitigation method and were unlinked from V3. The reader's limits_scope label based on them was replaced. All evidence is read from figures, with no tabulated values. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep with test error is reported.
No sweep over training epochs with test error is reported.
The study tests sample-wise error under its regression tasks and sampling procedures; it does not establish that increasing sample size raises error in other settings.
The study does not test risk as model-class capacity grows past an interpolation point.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of the peak location across axes.

The study varies nonlinear map complexity and discusses noise and regularization, but does not test the claimed label-noise or regularization dependence, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not re-express complexity using an effective parameter count.

relationships.condition: Standard random-sample training: GP with nonlinear coefficient L=5, 20, 50; DeepONet on MMT 8D data
relationships.reason: Test MSE and log-PDF error rise with added samples before falling again (r3–r8). For the DNN, the 1,500-sample error is not matched again until 15,000 (r15–r16). Evidence is figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Test MSE and log-density error rose before falling, and the DNN required 15,000 samples to regain its error at 1,500 samples.

relation.reason: The study directly measures test error against training-sample count and reports increases under standard training, alongside their mitigation by FOMO.

tranche.reason: Own sample-count experiments measure the effect in new regression settings: a nonlinear 1D GP problem and an 8D MMT DNN surrogate problem.

source_check.notes:
Section 3.1 calls the GP curves medians, whereas Figure 3's caption calls them means; minimum–maximum shading is consistent. The supplied text is the July 2024 v3 revision of the 2022 identifier.
The study establishes harmful sample-count increases but does not locate an interpolation threshold; Section 4 explicitly argues for a different explanation of the GP instability.

statements.correction: MMT inputs: 8D; standard training: 50–20,000 LHS samples; 25 experiments; normalized MSE and log-PDF error exhibit sample-wise double descent; Figure 4 reports means and minimum–maximum ranges; no interpolation threshold established; no US comparison reported.
statements.problem: The sample-wise error increases and reported uncertainty are supported, but this study contains no US acquisition comparison. Its standard DNN training uses LHS samples.

statements.correction: FOMO uses acquisition a(x)=w(x)σ²(x), with w(x)=p_x(x)/p_μ(μ); FOMO avoids the MMT error rise seen under standard LHS training; GP double descent is absent at L=0 and grows more severe with nonlinearity and heavy tails; Section 4 argues the GP instability does not coincide with a parameterization crossover.
statements.problem: The GP findings and FOMO avoidance of the LHS-training error rise are supported. The US comparison is not reported in this study.

statements.correction: DNN comparison: standard training on LHS samples versus FOMO sequential selection; FOMO avoids sample-wise double descent; GP instability severity increases with nonlinear coefficient and associated heavy tails; no US comparison reported.
statements.problem: Acquisition sensitivity and GP nonlinearity dependence are supported, but this study does not compare against US acquisition.
